title: Risk appetite, risk tolerance and the risk budget
blurb: Tell risk appetite (the business's attitude) from risk tolerance (the board's measurable threshold), and explain what the risk budget pays for.
question: The charity's trustees say they will take little risk with donors' money. The project board then sets a limit on aggregated threats of £25k. Which is the risk appetite and which is the risk tolerance?

teach.body: Formally: risk appetite is the amount and type of risk that the business is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives. In plain English: it is the organization's attitude to risk taking, decided above the project by the business (for example a chief executive and trustees). The project board applies that appetite to the project; it does not invent its own.

Formally: risk tolerance is a measurable threshold representing the tolerable range of outcomes for each objective 'at risk', in the same units used to measure performance for that objective. It is set by the project board based on the business's overall risk appetite. In plain English: appetite is the attitude; tolerance turns it into numbers that tell the project manager when to escalate.

levels.label: Project board
levels.sub: sets risk tolerance from that appetite

teach.caption: Risk is one of the seven tolerance areas: limits on the plan's aggregated risks.

teach.body: Formally: the risk budget is a sum of money to fund specific management responses to the project's threats and opportunities, for example the cost of a contingent plan if a risk materializes. In plain English: it is ring-fenced money for agreed risk responses. It is not for new requirements or approved changes to scope, which come from the change budget. Both budgets are optional and are set when preparing the budget for a plan.

head: Spending
Funded from
rows: Contingent plan triggered by a risk
Extra feature the users now want
Planned activity in the stage plan

teach.h: Worked scenario: a housing association refurbishment
teach.body: At Thornbury Homes, the board of directors states a cautious appetite: no project should put tenant safety or the year's maintenance budget at serious risk. Executive Olu Adeyemi's project board turns this into a risk tolerance: aggregated threat exposure must stay under £40k. Project manager Sian Morgan includes a £30k risk budget for a contingent plan if asbestos is found. When a request arrives to add new kitchen fittings, she explains that the risk budget cannot fund it: that is a change.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Appetite is the BUSINESS's attitude; tolerance is the measurable threshold set by the PROJECT BOARD based on that appetite. (2) Tolerance is not set from the project's own risk exposure; it comes from appetite. (3) The risk budget funds risk responses, the change budget funds approved changes.

items: Risk appetite: amount and type of risk the business will take; set by the business, applied by the board.
Risk tolerance: measurable threshold per objective at risk, in the objective's units.
The project board sets risk tolerance based on the business's risk appetite.
A forecast breach of risk tolerance is escalated (manage by exception).
Risk budget: funds specific responses to threats and opportunities, not changes.

summary: You can now tell risk appetite, the business's attitude to risk taking, from risk tolerance, the measurable threshold the project board sets from that appetite. You can also explain that the risk budget funds responses to threats and opportunities, while the change budget funds approved changes.

options: A measurable threshold for each objective at risk
Money set aside to fund specific risk responses
The amount and type of risk the business will take
The degree to which an objective is at risk
A.why: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the business is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives.

A.q: Who sets risk tolerance for a project?
options: The project manager, from the risk register
The project board, based on the risk appetite
The business layer, from the project brief
Project assurance, after reviewing exposure
A.why: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's overall risk appetite (manual 9.2.1).

whyNot.0: The project manager works within risk tolerance; the register records specific risks.
whyNot.2: The business sets the appetite; the board turns it into tolerance.
whyNot.3: Assurance supports the board; it does not set tolerances.

A.q: What is the risk budget used for?
options: To fund specific responses to threats and opportunities
To fund approved requests for change to the baseline
To cover activity costs in the current stage plan
To pay for the project board's assurance reviews
A.why: The risk budget funds specific management responses to threats and opportunities, such as contingent plans.

whyNot.1: Approved changes are funded by the change budget.
whyNot.2: Planned activity costs are part of the plan's main budget.
whyNot.3: Assurance costs are not what the risk budget is for.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Risk [?] is a measurable threshold representing the tolerable range of outcomes for each objective at risk.
options: appetite
exposure
proximity
tolerance
B.why: Risk tolerance is the measurable threshold, expressed in the units of the objective at risk.

whyNot.0: Appetite is the business's attitude, not a measurable threshold.
whyNot.1: Exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk.
whyNot.2: Proximity is how near in time a risk might occur.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Risk appetite is decided by the business.
2. Risk tolerance is set by the project manager.
3. Risk tolerance uses the same units as the objective it protects.
4. The risk budget funds new user requirements.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Appetite comes from the business (1) and tolerance is expressed in the objective's own units (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the project board sets risk tolerance.
whyNot.2: Both are false: the board sets tolerance, and new requirements are funded by the change budget.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: new requirements are changes, funded by the change budget.

B.q: A contingent plan to hire temporary generators is triggered when a power-supply threat occurs. Which budget should fund it?
options: The change budget
The activity budget
The cost tolerance
The risk budget
B.why: The risk budget covers the cost of specific responses, including contingent plans when a risk materializes.

whyNot.0: The change budget funds approved changes to the baseline.
whyNot.1: Activity costs cover planned work; contingent plans for risks are funded by the risk budget.
whyNot.2: Cost tolerance is a permitted deviation from the plan's cost, not a fund for risk responses.

C.q: A council's chief executive says the council is 'risk averse' on public safety. Which term describes this, and who applies it to the project?
options: Risk tolerance; the project manager
Risk appetite; the team manager
Risk exposure; project assurance
Risk appetite; the project board
C.why: The business's attitude to risk is its risk appetite, which the project board applies by setting risk tolerance.

whyNot.0: A stated attitude is appetite; tolerance is the board's measurable threshold.
whyNot.1: Team managers work within work package limits; they do not apply the appetite.
whyNot.2: Exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk.

C.q: A project board proposes setting risk tolerance by looking at the current risk exposure in the register. What should it base risk tolerance on instead?
options: The project manager's view of team capability
The proximity of the highest-scoring threats
The business's overall risk appetite
The size of the change budget
C.why: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's overall risk appetite, not on the project's current exposure.

whyNot.0: Team capability affects tailoring, not the basis of risk tolerance.
whyNot.1: Proximity affects when to respond, not the tolerance threshold.
whyNot.3: The change budget funds changes; it is not the basis of risk tolerance.

C.q: Aggregated threat exposure is forecast to exceed the stage's risk tolerance. Which principle is being applied when this is escalated, and to whom?
options: Manage by stages; to the business layer
Manage by exception; to the project board
Learn from experience; to project assurance
Manage by exception; to the team manager
C.why: Escalating a forecast breach of stage tolerance, including risk tolerance, applies manage by exception; the project manager escalates to the project board.

whyNot.0: Escalation of a tolerance breach is manage by exception, and stage-level breaches go to the board.
whyNot.2: Learn from experience concerns lessons, and assurance does not decide on exceptions.
whyNot.3: Escalation goes upwards to the board, not down to a team manager.

reteach.title: A household and its savings
reteach.question: A family says 'we don't gamble with the rent money', then agrees no single purchase over £300 without talking first. Which is appetite and which is tolerance?

blocks.body: 'We don't gamble with the rent money' is the appetite: an attitude to risk. '£300 before we talk' is the tolerance: a measurable threshold that triggers escalation. Money kept aside in case the boiler fails is like a risk budget: it pays for the response if the risk happens. A new sofa nobody planned is a change, paid from a different pot.

blocks.text: The board does not set the appetite; it applies the business's appetite by setting tolerance.

explain.body: The amount and type of risk the business is willing to take, set by the business and applied by the board.

options: The project manager
The project board
The business
The risk owner
test.why: Risk appetite is determined by the business and applied by the project board.

whyNot.0: The PM manages risks within tolerance.
whyNot.1: The board applies the appetite by setting tolerance; it does not determine it.
whyNot.3: A risk owner responds to one risk.

explain.body: A measurable threshold for each objective at risk, set by the board based on appetite.

options: As a general statement of attitude
In the units used for that objective
As the date of the next stage boundary
As a list of named risk owners
test.why: Risk tolerance uses the same units as for measuring performance against that objective.

whyNot.2: Stage boundaries are not how tolerance is expressed.
whyNot.3: Owners are recorded in the risk register.

explain.body: Money to fund specific responses to threats and opportunities, such as contingent plans.

test.q: Users ask for an extra report that was not in scope. Which budget would fund it if approved?
options: The risk budget
The tolerance reserve
The appetite fund
The change budget
test.why: An approved change to scope is funded from the change budget, not the risk budget.

whyNot.0: The risk budget funds responses to risks, not new requirements.
whyNot.1: Tolerance is a permitted deviation, not a fund for changes.
whyNot.2: Appetite is an attitude, not a budget.

explain.body: Risk is one of the seven tolerance areas. A forecast breach of risk tolerance is escalated.

test.q: What does risk tolerance describe for a plan?
options: Limits on the plan's aggregated risks
The plan's attitude to new suppliers
The date by which risks must be closed
The number of risks each owner may hold
test.why: Risk tolerance sets limits on the plan's aggregated risks.

whyNot.1: Attitudes to risk belong to the business's appetite.
whyNot.2: Tolerance is not a closure date.
whyNot.3: Tolerance is not a count of owners' risks.
